newsitem.title: USA: Clinton accused of using White House as Motel 1600.
newsitem.headline: Clinton accused of using White House as Motel 1600.

text.p: A Republican spokesman accused President Clinton of turning the White House into "Motel 1600", while Democratic Party Chairman Roy Romer urged Republicans to back bipartisan efforts to reform U.S. campaign finance laws, on a television broadcast on Saturday.

"We're all in a mess in this situation. Money is too influential," Romer, governor of Colorado, said on CNN's "Inside Politics," saying that Clinton and Vice President Al Gore were committed to enacting campaign finance reform legislation.

But Senate Ethics Committee Chairman Mitch McConnell said Democrats were trying to divert attention from their own violations of existing law and a majority of Republicans would not support constitutional limits on campaign spending.
Such limits, he said, amounted to allowing the government to curb political speech.
The Kentucky Republican said he had just two words for the president: "Reform yourself."

"We're not in a mess. You're the ones who turned the White House into a 'Motel 1600', renting out the Lincoln bedroom," McConnell told CNN's "Inside Politics." "There's no evidence that Republicans engaged in that kind of behaviour."
The reference was to published reports that major contributors to the Democratic Party were rewarded with nights in the Lincoln Bedroom of the White House.

Romer, elected to head the Democratic National Committee 10 days ago, said he instituted reforms at the party in the wake of several probes into questionable Clinton campaign fund-raising tactics during the last election.
The DNC returned large sums of money to contributors after reports that it improperly solicited funds from foreign business interests with a stake in U.S. trade policy.

"We have made mistakes at the Democratic National Committee and we're correcting them," Romer said, saying the DNC would no longer accept contributions from any foreign individuals or from subsidiaries of foreign-owned companies, even though these contributions are legal under current law.
He urged Republicans to adopt similar reforms, but McConnell said he saw no need to "go beyond existing law."
Romer appealed to Republicans to "leave this rhetoric that polarises aside," saying there were ways to reform campaign finance laws within the Constitution.
McConnell said "the notion that we're spending too much is nonsense," and said he did not expect bipartisan support for the legislation backed by Clinton.

The White House last week denied that its computerized database had been used to raise money for Clinton's re-election campaign or for any other unauthorised purposes, but sent Labour Secretary nominee Alexis Herman to Capitol Hill to explain her connection to a fund-raising event as director of the White House office of public liaison.

On Saturday, White House spokesman Lanny Davis said it was unfortunate that a New Jersey stock promoter, convicted and jailed for criminal securities fraud that benefited the Bonanno organised crime family, was invited to a coffee meeting with Clinton in December 1995.
